s: Great hailstones, each about the weight of a talent, fall from the sky on people. The plague is called exceedingly severe, and people blaspheme God because of it.

One of the seven bowl angels takes the narrator to see the judgment of the great prostitute, who sits on many waters. In the wilderness he sees a woman in purple and scarlet sitting on a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns. She holds a golden cup of abominations, bears a mystery name on her forehead, and is drunk with the blood of the saints and martyrs of Jesus. The angel explains the beast, the seven heads as mountains and kings, and the ten horns as ten kings who give their power to the beast and war against the Lamb, who overcomes them. The ten horns and the beast turn on the prostitute and destroy her, as God's words are accomplished, and she is identified as the great city that reigns over the kings of the earth.

The beast is scarlet, full of blasphemous names, and has seven heads and ten horns, and it carries the woman. The angel says it was, is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss and go to destruction, and that it is an eighth who is of the seven. The ten kings give their power and kingdom to it, and it joins them in hating and burning the prostitute.

l: angel (one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls), Revelation, Chapter 17
s: The angel calls the narrator and shows him the judgment of the great prostitute. He asks why the narrator wonders and then explains the mystery of the woman and the beast, the heads, the horns, and the waters, and identifies the woman as the great city.

The narrator is carried away in the Spirit into a wilderness and sees the woman on the beast. He wonders with great amazement at the sight of her drunk with the blood of the saints, and the angel then interprets the vision for him.
The ten kings will war against the Lamb, but the Lamb will overcome them. He is called Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called, chosen, and faithful.

They are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom but receive authority with the beast for one hour. They have one mind, give their power and authority to the beast, and war against the Lamb. With the beast they will hate the prostitute, make her desolate, strip her naked, eat her flesh, and burn her with fire, because God put it in their hearts to do his purpose.

l: judgment of the great prostitute, Revelation, Chapter 17
s: The angel offers to show this judgment to the narrator, who sees the prostitute sitting on many waters, which are peoples, multitudes, nations, and languages. The judgment is carried out when the ten horns and the beast hate her, make her desolate, strip her, eat her flesh, and burn her utterly with fire, until God's words are accomplished.

In Chapter 18, an angel with great authority descends from the sky and proclaims the fall of Babylon the great, which has become a habitation of demons and unclean spirits because the nations, kings, and merchants shared in her immorality and luxury. A voice from heaven calls God's people to come out of her so they do not share her sins or plagues, and commands that she be repaid double, since she boasts that she sits as a queen and will see no mourning. Her plagues of death, mourning, famine, and burning fire come in one day, and the kings, merchants, ship masters, and mariners stand far off lamenting the loss of her wealth and trade. Heaven, the saints, apostles, and prophets are told to rejoice because God has judged her. A mighty angel casts a millstone into the sea as a sign that Babylon will be thrown down and found no more, with all music, craft, light, and marriage ended in her, because of her sorcery and the blood of prophets, saints, and all the slain found in her.

Babylon the great is declared fallen and has become a habitation of demons and a prison of every unclean spirit and hated bird. She is accused of making the nations drink the wine of her immorality, enriching merchants, deceiving nations with sorcery, and bearing the blood of prophets, saints, and all the slain. She boasts that she sits a queen and will see no mourning, yet she is to be repaid double, burned, and made desolate in one hour.

l: angel (coming down out of the sky), Revelation, Chapter 18
s: This angel, having great authority, comes down out of the sky and lights the earth with his glory. He cries with a mighty voice that Babylon the great has fallen and describes her as a dwelling of demons and unclean spirits, because the nations, kings, and merchants shared in her immorality and luxury.

The mighty angel takes up a stone like a great millstone and casts it into the sea. He declares that Babylon will be thrown down with violence and found no more, and that music, craftsmen, the mill, lamplight, and the voices of bridegroom and bride will cease in her.
God has remembered Babylon's iniquities, and the Lord God who judged her is called strong. He has judged the saints' judgment on her, and heaven is told to rejoice over her fall.
A voice from heaven calls them to come out of Babylon so that they have no participation in her sins and do not receive her plagues. They are also told to repay her double according to her works.

l: kings of the earth, Revelation, Chapter 18
s: The kings of the earth committed sexual immorality and lived wantonly with Babylon. They will weep and wail when they see the smoke of her burning, standing far away in fear of her torment and lamenting that her judgment came in one hour.

l: merchants of the earth, Revelation, Chapter 18
s: The merchants of the earth grew rich from Babylon's luxury, and her fall leaves no one to buy their goods, which include metals, gems, fabrics, spices, foods, animals, chariots, and people's bodies and souls. They stand far away weeping and mourning, lamenting that such great riches were made desolate in an hour. Babylon's rulers are described as their princes.

l: ship masters and mariners, Revelation, Chapter 18
s: Every ship master, everyone who sails, the mariners, and all who earn their living by sea stand far away as Babylon burns. They cry out 'What is like the great city?', cast dust on their heads, and weep and mourn because all who had ships at sea were made rich by her wealth, which is made desolate in one hour.

Babylon's destruction comes in one day and one hour, with death, mourning, famine, and burning with fire. It is illustrated by the mighty angel's millstone cast into the sea, and it silences all music, craft, light, and wedding voices in her. Heaven, the saints, apostles, and prophets are told to rejoice, while kings, merchants, and sailors lament from afar.

A great multitude in heaven, together with the twenty-four elders and four living creatures, praises God for judging the great prostitute and avenging his servants, and announces that the wedding of the Lamb has come and his wife has made herself ready in fine linen. An angel tells John to write a blessing on those invited to the wedding supper, and refuses John's attempt to worship him, saying to worship God. John then sees heaven opened and a rider on a white horse called Faithful and True, the Word of God, and KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS, who judges, makes war, and is followed by armies in heaven. An angel in the sun summons the birds to the great supper of God, and the beast, the kings of the earth, and their armies gather to make war against the rider. The beast and the false prophet are thrown alive into the lake of fire, and the rest are killed by the sword from the rider's mouth while the birds feed on their flesh.

God is praised by the heavenly multitude for salvation, power, glory, and true and righteous judgments, and is worshiped by the elders and living creatures as he sits on the throne. He is called the Lord our God, the Almighty, who reigns, and the angel tells John to worship him. The wine press of the fierceness of his wrath is trodden, and the supper that bears his name is announced for the birds.
The wedding of the Lamb is announced as having come, and his wife has made herself ready. A blessing is pronounced on those invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb.

l: Faithful and True (rider on the white horse), Revelation, Chapter 19
s: Heaven opens and he appears on a white horse, called Faithful and True, judging and making war in righteousness. He has eyes like a flame of fire, many crowns, a name no one knows but himself, a garment sprinkled with blood, and the name The Word of God. A sharp sword comes from his mouth, he will rule the nations with an iron rod, he treads the wine press of God's wrath, and he bears the name KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS on his garment and thigh. He defeats the beast and false prophet, and kills the rest with the sword from his mouth.

l: great multitude in heaven, Revelation, Chapter 19
s: The great multitude cries Hallelujah, praising God for salvation, power, and glory and for his true and righteous judgments on the great prostitute. Their voice is like many waters and mighty thunders as they declare that the Lord God Almighty reigns and call for rejoicing because the wedding of the Lamb has come.
She is said to have corrupted the earth with her sexual immorality and to have shed the blood of God's servants. God has judged her and avenged his servants, and her smoke goes up forever and ever.

l: bride (New Jerusalem as a bride), Revelation, Chapter 19
s: The Lamb's wife has made herself ready for the wedding. It was given to her to array herself in bright, pure, fine linen, which is the righteous acts of the saints.
The armies in heaven, clothed in white, pure, fine linen, follow the rider called Faithful and True on white horses. The text records no fighting by them; the rider's sword kills the rest.

The beast is seen gathered with the kings of the earth and their armies to make war against the rider on the horse and his army. He is taken and thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur.

l: kings of the earth and their armies, Revelation, Chapter 19
s: The kings of the earth and their armies gather with the beast to make war against him who sat on the horse and his army. They are killed with the sword that comes out of the rider's mouth, and the birds are filled with their flesh.

The false prophet is identified as the one who worked signs in the beast's sight, deceiving those who had received the mark of the beast and worshiped his image. He is taken with the beast and thrown alive into the lake of fire that burns with sulfur.

An angel descends from heaven with the key of the abyss and a great chain, seizes the dragon (the old serpent, the devil and Satan), and binds him in the sealed abyss for a thousand years so he cannot deceive the nations. Those who were beheaded for their testimony and refused the beast, its image, and its mark sit on thrones, live, and reign with Christ for a thousand years in the first resurrection, while the rest of the dead wait until the thousand years end. After the thousand years Satan is released, deceives the nations Gog and Magog, and gathers them for war against the camp of the saints and the beloved city, but fire from God devours them. The devil is thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet already are. Then, before a great white throne, the dead are judged by their works from the books and the book of life, and Death, Hades, and anyone not written in the book of life are cast into the lake of fire.

l: angel (who came down out of heaven), Revelation, Chapter 20
s: The angel comes down out of heaven holding the key of the abyss and a great chain. He seizes the dragon, binds him for a thousand years, casts him into the abyss, and shuts and seals it.

The abyss is the place into which the dragon is cast, shut, and sealed so that he cannot deceive the nations for a thousand years. Its key is held by the descending angel. Satan is released from this prison after the thousand years.

Christ is the one with whom the martyred and faithful souls live and reign for a thousand years. The blessed who share in the first resurrection will be priests of God and of Christ and reign with him.
God sends fire down out of heaven that devours the nations surrounding the saints' camp. The faithful who share in the first resurrection will be his priests, along with Christ's.

The thousand years is the period during which Satan is bound in the abyss and the faithful reign with Christ. The rest of the dead do not live until it ends. After it, Satan is released for a short time.

l: martyrs and faithful saints who reign with Christ, Revelation, Chapter 20
s: They include those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and the word of God, and those who did not worship the beast or its image or receive its mark. They sit on thrones with judgment given to them, live and reign with Christ for a thousand years, and are blessed, holy, and priests of God and Christ, with the second death having no power over them.

The first resurrection is when the martyrs and faithful come to life and reign with Christ, while the rest of the dead stay dead until the thousand years finish. Those who share in it are called blessed and holy, and the second death has no power over them.

Gog and Magog are the nations in the four corners of the earth that Satan deceives after his release. They are gathered for war in a number like the sand of the sea, and are devoured by fire from heaven.

l: the final war against the saints, Revelation, Chapter 20
s: After Satan's release, the deceived nations go up over the width of the earth and surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city. Fire coming down from God out of heaven devours them, and the devil who deceived them is then thrown into the lake of fire.

The lake of fire and sulfur is where the devil is thrown, joining the beast and the false prophet, to be tormented day and night forever. Death and Hades are also thrown into it, and it is named the second death. Anyone not found written in the book of life is cast into it.
The great white throne is the seat of the one before whose face the earth and sky flee away, leaving no place for them. The dead, great and small, stand before it to be judged.

The dead are judged before the great white throne, with books opened and the book of life, each according to his works. The sea, Death, and Hades give up their dead for this judgment. Afterward Death and Hades and all not found in the book of life are cast into the lake of fire.

The rest of the dead do not live until the thousand years are finished. Later the dead, great and small, are given up by the sea, Death, and Hades, and stand before the throne to be judged by their works as written in the books.
The book of life is opened, separately from the other books, at the judgment before the great white throne. Anyone not found written in it is cast into the lake of fire.

The narrator sees a new heaven and a new earth, with the first ones and the sea gone, and the holy city New Jerusalem descending from God like an adorned bride. A voice from heaven declares that God will dwell with people, wipe away every tear, and end death, mourning, crying, and pain. The one on the throne says he makes all things new, names himself the Alpha and Omega, promises the water of life to the thirsty and sonship to those who overcome, and consigns the cowardly, unbelieving, and other wrongdoers to the lake of fire, the second death. One of the seven angels with the bowls then carries the narrator in the Spirit to a high mountain and shows him the bride, the Lamb's wife, measuring the city with a golden reed. The city is described with a wall of jasper, twelve pearl gates bearing the tribes of Israel's names, twelve jeweled foundations bearing the names of the Apostles of the Lamb, and gold streets, and it has no temple or sun because God and the Lamb are its temple and light, while the nations walk in its light and only those written in the Lamb's book of life may enter.

New Jerusalem, the holy city, is seen coming down out of heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband, and is identified as the bride, the Lamb's wife. It is square, with equal length, width, and height, a jasper wall with twelve gates of pearl and twelve foundations of precious stones, and pure gold like clear glass for the city and its street. It has no temple, sun, or moon, since God and the Lamb are its temple and light, its gates are never shut, and only those written in the Lamb's book of life may enter.

God is announced as dwelling with people, being their God, wiping away every tear, and ending death, mourning, crying, and pain. He who sits on the throne declares he is making all things new, calls himself the Alpha and Omega, the Beginning and the End, promises the water of life to the thirsty, and says the overcomer will be his son. The city has his glory as its light, and he, the Lord God the Almighty, is its temple together with the Lamb.

The Lamb is called the husband of the bride, as the city is shown as the Lamb's wife. The twelve foundations of the city wall bear the names of his twelve Apostles. Together with the Lord God the Almighty he is the city's temple, he is its lamp, and his book of life lists those who may enter.

l: new heaven and new earth, Revelation, Chapter 21
s: The narrator sees a new heaven and a new earth because the first heaven and the first earth have passed away, and the sea is no more. The first things passing away is tied to the end of death, mourning, crying, and pain, and to God making all things new.

The narrator, speaking in the first person, sees the new heaven and earth and the holy city and hears the loud voice from heaven. He is told to write because the words are faithful and true. He is carried away in the Spirit to a great and high mountain, where he is shown the city and watches its measuring, and he notes that he saw no temple in it.

l: angel (one of the seven angels with the bowls), Revelation, Chapter 21
s: One of the seven angels who held the seven bowls of the last plagues comes and speaks with the narrator, inviting him to see the bride, the Lamb's wife. He carries the narrator to a high mountain and shows him the holy city. He measures the city, its gates, and its walls with a golden reed, and his measure, by a man's measure, is that of an angel.

In Revelation 22, an angel shows John a river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on either side of it, and describes the city where there is no curse and no night. The angel affirms that the words are faithful and true and rebuffs John when he falls to worship him, saying he is a fellow bondservant and that God alone should be worshiped. Jesus speaks, declaring that he is coming soon with his reward, that he is the Alpha and the Omega, and that he is the root and offspring of David and the Bright and Morning Star. The Spirit and the bride invite the thirsty to take the water of life freely. A warning is given against adding to or taking away from the words of the book, and the book closes with John's prayer "Come, Lord Jesus" and a blessing of grace on the saints.

God is described as the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets, who sent his angel to show his bondservants what must happen soon. His throne, shared with the Lamb, is in the city, and he will illuminate his people so that they need no lamp or sun. The angel tells John to worship God alone, and God will add plagues to anyone who adds to the book's words or take away the share of anyone who removes from them.

Jesus declares that he is coming soon with his reward to repay each person according to his work, and calls himself the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End. He states that he sent his angel to testify these things to the assemblies, and names himself the root and offspring of David and the Bright and Morning Star. The text also refers to him as the Lamb on the throne with God, and closes with "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all the saints."

John identifies himself as the one who heard and saw these things. He fell down to worship before the feet of the angel and was told not to do so. He is instructed not to seal up the words of the prophecy, and he ends with the cry "Yes, come, Lord Jesus!"

l: angel (who showed John these things), Revelation, Chapter 22
s: The angel shows John the river of the water of life and the tree of life, and tells him the words are faithful and true. When John falls at his feet to worship, the angel forbids it, saying he is a fellow bondservant with John, the prophets, and those who keep the book's words, and commands John to worship God. Jesus says he sent this angel to testify to the assemblies.

The tree of life stands on both sides of the river in the middle of the street, bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding fruit every month. Its leaves are for the healing of the nations. Those who do God's commandments have the right to it, and God will take away the share in it from anyone who removes words from the book.

The holy city contains the river of the water of life and the throne of God and of the Lamb, and there is no curse and no night in it. Those who do his commandments may enter by its gates, while the dogs, sorcerers, sexually immoral, murderers, idolaters, and lovers of falsehood remain outside. Anyone who takes away from the book's words loses his part in it.

His servants will serve him in the city, see his face, and bear his name on their foreheads. They will reign forever and ever, with the Lord God as their light. The angel counts himself a fellow bondservant with them.

l: book of this prophecy, Revelation, Chapter 22
s: The book is declared faithful and true, and its words are not to be sealed up because the time is at hand. Blessing is promised to those who keep its words. Anyone who adds to it will receive the plagues written in it, and anyone who takes away from it will lose his part in the tree of life and the holy city.

Jesus announces three times in this chapter that he is coming soon, in verses 7, 12, and 20. His coming brings a reward that repays each person according to his work, and blessing for those who keep the words of the prophecy. The book ends with the response "Yes, come, Lord Jesus!"

This is the Book of Judith, sixteen chapters telling how the Israelite town of Bethulia is saved from an Assyrian invasion by a widow named Judith. Chapter 1 sets the stage: Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians at Nineveh, defeats and kills Arphaxad of the Medes after western peoples ignore his call for help, and he vows vengeance on them. In chapters 2 and 3 he sends his chief captain Holofernes with a vast army; it ravages nations, receives submissions from coastal peoples, and destroys their gods and groves so that Nebuchadnezzar alone is worshipped. Chapter 4 shows Judea fearing for Jerusalem and the temple; the high priest Joakim orders the hill passes at Bethulia held, and all Israel fasts and prays in sackcloth. In chapters 5 and 6 Achior, leader of the Ammonites, tells Holofernes that Israel can be beaten only if it has sinned against its God. Holofernes mocks him, declares Nebuchadnezzar the only god, and sends Achior to Bethulia, where the rulers Ozias, Chabris and Charmis welcome him. Chapter 7 has Holofernes besiege the town and cut off its water; after thirty-four days the thirsty people demand surrender, and Ozias asks for five more days. In chapter 8 Judith, a wealthy, devout widow, rebukes the rulers for testing God and announces a deed to be remembered through all generations. She prays in chapter 9 for God to strike the enemy by the hand of a woman. In chapters 10 to 12 she dresses beautifully, goes with her maid to the Assyrian camp, and wins Holofernes's trust with a false plan to lead him through Judea. She stays three days, then dines at his feast, where he drinks heavily. In chapter 13 she beheads the drunken Holofernes with his own sword and carries the head back to Bethulia, where Ozias blesses her. In chapter 14 the head is hung on the wall, Achior sees it and converts, is circumcised and joins Israel, and the Assyrians, finding Holofernes dead, fall into panic. Chapter 15 describes their flight, the pursuit and slaughter by Israel, the plunder of the camp, and Joakim's blessing; Holofernes's belongings are given to Judith, and she leads the women in dance. Chapter 16 closes with her song of thanksgiving, the worship and offerings at Jerusalem, and her dedication of Holofernes's goods to the Lord. She returns to Bethulia, stays unmarried, frees her maid, and dies at 105, buried with her husband Manasses, and Israel is left unthreatened in her lifetime and long after.

Nebuchadnezzar is the king of the Assyrians, reigning from Nineveh, who styles himself the great king and lord of all the earth. The records open with him making war on Arphaxad and summoning western peoples, who refuse him. Angered, he swears vengeance by his throne and kingdom. He then defeats Arphaxad in the seventeenth year, captures Ecbatana, kills Arphaxad in the mountains of Ragau, and returns to Nineveh to feast with his vast multinational army for one hundred twenty days. He next convenes his great men, who decree destruction of all flesh that did not follow his word, and charges Holofernes with a campaign against the west. His aims grow explicitly divine: destroying the land's gods so all nations worship him alone and call upon him as a god. Later chapters show him through Holofernes, who calls him lord of all the earth and the only god, says his words will not be in vain, and promises that those who serve him will not be hurt. He remains offstage, a distant, absolute power.

Arphaxad, king of the Medes reigning in Ecbatana, fortified the city with great hewn-stone walls, towers and gates; Nebuchadnezzar defeated his army, captured him in Ragau's mountains, and killed him with darts.

The Assyrians are the enemy force threatening Bethulia, led by the chief captain Holofernes. Ozias has promised to surrender the town to them after five days, and Judith warns that defeat would mean captivity, plunder of the sanctuary and dishonor. They are portrayed as mighty, multiplied in power, proud of horse, rider and footmen, and trusting in shield, spear, bow and sling, yet ignorant that the Lord breaks battles. They intend to defile the tabernacle and destroy the altar's horn. Later, an Assyrian watch meets Judith, marvels at her beauty, and escorts her to Holofernes' tent amid an excited camp.

Ecbatana is Arphaxad's Median city, fortified with tall hewn-stone walls, hundred-cubit towers and army-sized gates; Nebuchadnezzar then captures its towers, plunders its streets, and turns its beauty into shame.

l: war between Nebuchadnezzar and Arphaxad, Judith
s: War fought on the great plain at the borders of Ragau, where Arphaxad gathered allies from many regions and nations. In the seventeenth year Nebuchadnezzar prevailed, routed his army, took his cities including Ecbatana, and killed Arphaxad in the mountains of Ragau.

Jerusalem is the seat of Joakim the high priest and of the senate of all the people of Israel, whose members carry out his command. Its inhabitants fall prostrate before the temple in sackcloth and ashes, and they join the fasting. Jerusalem is where the priests stand before God, and Judith says the Bethulians have sent people there to get permission from the council of elders to consume the sanctified food. She claims that people there have done the same thing. She promises to lead Holofernes through Judea to Jerusalem and set his throne in its midst.

Judea is where the children of Israel live, newly returned from captivity and recently gathered. Its entrance is through the hill-country ascents, and the whole land keeps fasting for many days before the sanctuary.

l: peoples of the western lands (Nebuchadnezzar's summoned), Judith
s: disposition_toward_nebuchadnezzar disregard [refused his summons to war and were not afraid of him] Nebuchadnezzar sends messengers to peoples across Persia, Cilicia, Damascus, Libanus, the sea coast, Carmel, Gilead, Galilee, Esdraelon, Samaria, Jerusalem, and Egypt up to the borders of Ethiopia. They make light of his command, do not fear him, and turn his messengers away with disgrace, which provokes his oath of vengeance against Cilicia, Damascus, Syria, Moab, Ammon, Judea, and Egypt.

Holofernes is the chief captain of Nebuchadnezzar's army, second in rank to the king and leader of the army of Asshur. He is commanded to go against the western country, sparing those who yield and slaying those who resist. He musters the army, leaves Nineveh and campaigns destructively to the sea coast. Receiving submissions, he sets garrisons in the high cities and takes chosen men as allies. Though welcomed with garlands, dances and timbrels, he casts down borders and cuts down sacred groves, tasked with destroying the gods of the land. He camps between Geba and Scythopolis for a month to gather baggage. The people of Judea hear he has destroyed the temples of the nations and are terrified. Told that Israel has fortified the hill country, he grows angry and questions Moab's princes, Ammon's captains and the coastal governors. After hearing Achior, he rebukes him, scorns Israel's God, declares Nebuchadnezzar the only god, and sends Achior to Bethulia to be destroyed with the Israelites. He moves against Bethulia, posts garrisons over its springs, and on the advice of the rulers of Esau, Moab and the coast chooses siege over battle. Judith then comes to him with words of truth. He receives her before his tent with silver lamps going before him, promises her safety, praises her beauty and wisdom, and says her God will be his God and she will live in Nebuchadnezzar's palace. He orders his guards not to stop her nightly outings. On the fourth day he holds a feast for his servants only and sends Bagoas to bring her, having long watched to deceive her. Ravished by her, he drinks more wine than ever before. Lying drunk on his bed under the canopy, with his sword at the bedpost, he is beheaded by Judith with his own sword, and she says the Lord struck him by a woman's hand. Bagoas finds him dead and headless on the threshold, and the camp falls into turmoil. Achior is brought to see the man who despised Israel. Later the song, without naming him, says the mighty enemy was made weak by Judith's beauty and struck through the neck. His belongings are dedicated to the Lord, and his canopy is given as a gift.

Asshur is the vast army of King Nebuchadnezzar, led by Holofernes. It is described as 120,000 chosen footmen and 12,000 horsemen (elsewhere 170,000 footmen), with camels, donkeys, mules, livestock, rations and treasure, accompanied by a countless company of nations like locusts. It destroys, burns and plunders many lands. It then camps in the valley by the fountain near Bethulia, seizing waters and springs, covering the plain, and surrounding the town for thirty-four days. Its parts include captains, tribunes and the Assyrian camp. The turning point comes when Holofernes' death is discovered: the rulers tear their tunics, a great cry rises, and, as Judith had predicted, fear falls on the camp. The army flees across plain and hill country, is slaughtered past Damascus, and its camp is plundered, enriching the Israelites. Israel's lowly ones shouted and the enemy perished by the army of the Lord, while Persians and Medes quaked at Judith's daring.

l: people of the west country, Judith
s: disobeys Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians [commandment of his mouth] The people of the west country are accused of disobeying the king's command and are to be told to prepare earth and water. Many are destroyed, including Put, Lud, the children of Rasses and Ishmael, and Midian, while the coastal cities of Sidon, Tyre, Sur, Ocina, Jemnaan, Azotus and Ascalon are seized by fear and dread.

l: Nebuchadnezzar's campaign of vengeance and conquest, Judith
s: has_target people of the west country [all the west country] The campaign is decreed in the eighteenth year as vengeance on all the land. It begins from Nineveh toward Bectileth and Cilicia, crosses the Euphrates and Mesopotamia, burns Midian's tents and the fields of the plain of Damascus at wheat harvest, and reaches the sea coast, where its terror falls on the coastal cities.

is_sent_by people of the coastal land The messengers are sent with words of peace to Holofernes. They carry a message that their people are servants of Nebuchadnezzar and that their dwellings, land, fields, flocks, herds and cities lie before him to be used as he pleases. They come to Holofernes and declare these words to him.

l: people of the coastal land (senders of the messengers), Judith
s: The people send messengers to offer submission, and when Holofernes comes they receive him with garlands, dances and timbrels, along with all the country round about. Despite this, their borders are cast down and their sacred groves cut down, and garrisons are set in their high cities, from which chosen men are taken as allies.

l: submission of the messengers' people, Judith
s: is_a offer of peace The people offer themselves, their dwellings, country, wheat fields, flocks, herds, tents and cities as servants of Nebuchadnezzar, to be dealt with as Holofernes sees fit. Holofernes accepts the offer by coming to their land, but it does not spare them from garrisons, conscription of allies, and the destruction of their borders and sacred groves.

l: campaign of destruction and worship of Nebuchadnezzar, Judith
s: A campaign given to Holofernes to destroy all the gods of the land so every nation worships Nebuchadnezzar only. He casts down borders and cuts down sacred groves, then advances toward Esdraelon and Judea's ridge, pausing a month at a camp.

The children of Israel are a people of Judea, dwelling in the hill country and in Bethulia, who worship the God of heaven and hold Jerusalem and the holy house at the top of Zion as their sanctuary and possession. Achior describes them as descended from the Chaldeans, who left their fathers' gods, sojourned in Mesopotamia, Canaan and Egypt, were enslaved and freed, took the hill country, were later taken captive for leaving God's way, and have now returned to their God and settled Jerusalem. Their central safeguard is stated by Judith: they will not be punished or defeated unless they sin against their God. The story begins with fear at Holofernes' approach. Obeying Joakim's command, they occupy the mountain tops, shut the passages, fortify villages and hilltops, store supplies and set up barricades, while humbling themselves in sackcloth, ashes and fasting, crying to God not to give their families and sanctuary to the nations. Holofernes' men dismiss them as powerless. At Bethulia they receive Achior, worship God, and pray for pity. Terrified by the enemy multitude, they keep watch and cry to the Lord; besieged and weakened by thirst, they turn on their rulers and demand surrender, but agree to wait five more days. Their elders pray that Judith's purposes bring glory to Israel and exaltation to Jerusalem. The Assyrians marvel that Israel has such women, and Judith's words to Holofernes affirm that the sword prevails only if they sin. The turning point comes with the Assyrians in flight: every Israelite warrior rushes out, pursues them past Damascus and strikes them to Chobai, then returns to take spoils. They follow Judith in armor and garlands, singing, worship and sacrifice in Jerusalem, feast three months, and return to their inheritances. The house of Israel mourns Judith seven days, and in her days and long after no one makes them afraid.

The Jerusalem temple, with altar and vessels, was sanctified after being profaned. Fearing for it, the people prostrate, drape the altar in sackcloth, and pray it not be profaned again, while Joakim and priests keep offerings.

The Lord, titled Almighty and God of Israel, is portrayed as a great, glorious, invincible God who crushes battles and creates all things by his word and spirit. Early, Israel cries to him and he hears their affliction. Later, Judith's song praises him for delivering her and destroying Asshur's army through a woman, as merciful to those who fear him, and a future judge of hostile nations.

Joakim is the high priest at Jerusalem who orders Bethulia and Betomesthaim to seize the hill-country ascents, and the people obey; he and the priests don sackcloth and ashes, offer sacrifices, and cry to the Lord for Israel.

Bethulia is a hill-country city on a mountain, inhabited by the children of Israel and ruled by Ozias, Chabris, and Charmis. It has gates guarded by watchmen, and springs flow from the foot of the mountain beneath it. Its men first repel Holofernes' servants with slingers and receive the freed Achior in assembly. The enemy host then surrounds the city and seizes the springs and ascents. Over thirty-four days the cisterns empty and people collapse from thirst. The leaders swear to surrender after five days, but Judith, the city's widow of Manasses, warns that its fall would mean the capture of all Judea and the plundering of the sanctuary. Ozias and the elders open the gate for her and her maid, and the men watch her descend the mountain and cross the valley. She returns, calls the watchmen to open the gates, and the people run together, light a fire, worship God, and bless her after she shows the head. The enemy then flee, and Bethulia's people plunder the camp of Asshur, becoming exceedingly rich.

The hill country near Bethulia, once desolate, was possessed and resettled by the children of Israel. Its narrow ascents form the entrance into Judea, where two men at most fit, so Joakim orders them seized. Israel then shuts the passages and fortifies the hilltops near Holofernes, whose men vow to attack and make Israel prey.

Sackcloth is put on the loins of the people, their wives, children, cattle, sojourners, hirelings, and servants, and is spread out before the Lord and placed around the altar. Joakim and the priests also wear it as a sign of humbling.

All Israel cries to God earnestly and with one consent, with ashes on their heads, that their children, wives, cities, and sanctuary not be given to destruction or reproach. The Lord hears, and the people continue fasting many days in Judea and Jerusalem before the sanctuary.

Achior is an Ammonite, leader of all the children of Ammon, and also addressed alongside the children of Moab. In Chapter 5 he tells Holofernes the truth, giving a history of Israel and advising attack only if Israel has sinned against its God. His words provoke anger and calls for him to be cut to pieces. In Chapter 6 Holofernes calls him a hireling of Ammon and sends him to Bethulia. He is bound and left at the foot of the hill, freed by Israelites, brought before Ozias and the rulers, praised, and taken into Ozias's house. In Chapter 14 he sees Holofernes' head, faints, revives, and blesses Judith. Having seen what God had done, he believes, is circumcised, and joins the house of Israel to this day.

The God of Israel, called the Lord, is presented as the Most High God, creator of the heavens, earth and waters, King of all creation, and the sole protector of the race of Israel. He hates iniquity, judges with foreknowledge, has planned past, present and future, and cannot be searched out, threatened or won over like a human. His name rests in the tabernacle. He is a God of the afflicted, helper of the oppressed and weak, protector of the forsaken and savior of the hopeless, and the people of Bethulia worship him exclusively, with no gods made with hands. The records unfold in a sequence of scenes. Achior first recounts how the God of heaven led Israel out of Mesopotamia to Canaan, struck Egypt with plagues, dried up the Red Sea and cast out peoples, staying with Israel while they did not sin; if Israel is without lawlessness, he will defend them. Holofernes then mocks him, while besieged Bethulia cries out to him all night. The people think he has sold them into enemy hands to punish their sins, but Ozias says he will turn his mercy toward them. Judith describes him as Lord Almighty who may help or destroy when he chooses and who tests those near him, as with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. She prays to the God of Simeon, who gave a sword for vengeance, asking him to break the Assyrians' strength and show all nations that no one else protects Israel. She tells Holofernes that God sent her to do astonishing things, and Holofernes says her God will become his God. Finally, after Judith prays to the Lord God of all power and of Israel for strength, the deed is done. Judith, the people and Ozias credit him with the victory, saying he showed his power, did not withdraw his mercy, humbled the enemies of his people, and directed Judith to cut off the enemy prince's head. The people worship him.

l: Israelite sin and its consequences, Judith
s: results_in destruction in battle and captivity [when they departed from God's way] Achior teaches that Israel prospered while it did not sin before its God, because God who hates iniquity was with them. When they departed from the way he appointed, they were destroyed in many severe battles, led captive into a land not theirs, their temple was razed, and their cities were taken. He proposes that Holofernes find out whether they now stumble in sin before attacking, and pass by if there is no lawlessness among them.

Ozias, son of Micah of the tribe of Simeon, is one of Bethulia's three rulers and elders, alongside Chabris and Charmis. He trusts that God will show mercy. He first hosts Achior the Ammonite in his house and feasts the elders. Later the people blame the rulers for not seeking peace with the Assyrians. Ozias urges courage, asks for five more days, and swears to deliver the city if no help comes. When Judith rebukes him, he acknowledges her wisdom and godliness, explains that the thirsty people compelled the oath, asks her to pray for rain, and blesses her above all women before sending her off in peace.

Holofernes' servants are commanded to take Achior to Bethulia and deliver him to the Israelites. They bring him to the springs below the city, are driven back by slingers, then bind Achior, leave him at the foot of the hill, and return to their lord.

The springs, including the one flowing from the foot of the mountain, supply all the inhabitants of Bethulia. Holofernes searches them out and garrisons them, and the Ammonites and Assyrians then seize them, cutting off the city's water.

Ozias, Chabris, and Charmis, the elders of the city, are summoned by Judith's maid and are told that their word before the people was not right. They accept her commission, agree not to inquire into her act, say 'Go in peace,' and return to their stations.

The children of Esau are allies of Holofernes whose rulers, with Moab's leaders and coastal captains, advise starving Israel of water rather than fighting it. The plan is adopted, and they join the Ammonites camping near Dothaim around Bethulia.

Holofernes besieges Bethulia, seizing springs and hills so none can leave; after thirty-four days water runs dry, the people demand surrender, and Ozias wins a five-day delay, promising surrender if no help comes.

Judith is a beautiful, wealthy, devout Hebrew widow from Bethulia, daughter of Merari and widow of Manasses. She has lived three years and four months in widowhood, in a tent on her roof, wearing sackcloth and fasting except on Sabbaths, new moons and feasts. No evil is spoken of her because she fears God exceedingly. She is attended by a maid who oversees all she has. The story opens with her rebuking the elders for testing God with their oath, and she tells them the Lord will deliver Israel by her hand. She prays with ashes on her head, asking God to make her speech and deceit a wound to those who plot against his covenant and house. She then discards her widow's clothing, dresses beautifully, and goes with her maid to the Assyrian camp, saying she is a Hebrew fleeing her people. Brought to Holofernes, she flatters him, promises to lead him to Jerusalem, and is praised by him and his servants as unmatched in beauty and wisdom. For three days she stays in the camp, eating only her own provisions, and goes out each night to wash at the fountain and pray. At the feast she is left alone with the drunken Holofernes, prays for strength, and cuts off his head with his sword. She carries it in her food bag back to Bethulia, where Ozias blesses her above all women. She has the head hung on the wall, outlines the plan that makes the Assyrians flee, and tells the people all she did. Achior bows at her feet and blesses her. Joakim the high priest and the elders bless her as the exaltation of Jerusalem and great glory of Israel, and she receives Holofernes' tent and furnishings. She leads the women in a dance and begins a song of thanksgiving, crediting the Lord with using her beauty against the enemy. She dedicates Holofernes' belongings and canopy to the Lord and returns to Bethulia, honored in all the land. She never knew a man after Manasses died. She frees her maid, distributes her goods to kin, dies at 105, and is buried in Manasses' cave.

suffers_from water shortage [fainting from lack of water] Judith's kindred are told to hang the head on the wall and to arm themselves at dawn and go out as if descending to the plain, without actually going down. They shout and rejoice when Judith finishes her account, then hang the head and go out by bands to the mountain ascents with their weapons.

has_condition deliver Bethulia to the Assyrians after five days [unless the Lord helps within these days] Ozias's oath to deliver the city to the Assyrians after five days unless God helps is condemned by Judith as wrongly placed between God and the leaders, and as testing God. Ozias defends it as forced by the thirsty people and says it cannot be broken, so Judith works within its time limit.

Judith's planned deed, announced in Chapter 8: she and her maid will leave the city gate, and the Lord will deliver Israel by her hand within the oath's days. She forbids the rulers to inquire; she will reveal it only when finished.

Judith's prayer, addressed to Lord God in Chapter 9, recalls Simeon's vengeance, God's foreknowledge and care for the weak, and the Assyrian threat, then petitions him to break the Assyrians by a woman's hand, so all nations know Israel's protector.

Judith's adornment is her beautifying attire and jewelry, meant to deceive the eyes of men. In Chapter 10 she washes, anoints, braids her hair, and dons a tiara, garments of gladness from Manasses' days, sandals, anklet, bracelets, rings, earrings; it astonishes elders, Assyrian watch, camp, Holofernes' servants.

l: Israelites' sin of consuming sanctified food, Judith
s: is_forbidden_by God [God's laws] Judith claims that, because their food and water have failed, her people mean to kill their livestock and eat what God forbade them by his laws, including first fruits of the grain and tithes of wine and oil reserved for the priests. She says they have sought permission from the elders in Jerusalem and that, once they act, they will be given over to Holofernes to be destroyed the same day.

Bagoas is a eunuch in charge of all that Holofernes has, serving him as lord and attendant who wakes him and guards his tent. In Chapter 12 he persuades Judith to dine with Holofernes, promising her honor. In Chapter 14 he finds Holofernes dead and headless, weeps, tears his garments, discovers Judith gone, and cries that a Hebrew woman has shamed Nebuchadnezzar's house.

excludes officers [none were called] On the fourth day Holofernes makes a feast for his own servants only, calling none of the officers. Judith attends at his invitation via Bagoas, sits on fleeces beside him, and eats and drinks what her servant prepared. Holofernes grows delighted and drinks exceedingly much wine, more than on any day since his birth.

Judith declines Holofernes' delicacies and wine, saying she cannot eat them lest there be an occasion of stumbling, and that provision will be made from what came with her. When Holofernes asks what will happen when it runs out, she says it will not be used up until the Lord works by her hand. She eats her food toward evening each day and at the feast eats and drinks what her servant prepared.

Holofernes' head is the severed trophy of the enemy captain. Judith's maid places it in her food bag; at Bethulia's gate Judith shows it as proof of his death, and the people worship God. It is displayed before the assembly, making Achior faint, then hung on the city wall, alarming the Assyrians.

Judith beheads the drunken Holofernes on his bed: after praying for strength, she grasps his hair, strikes his neck twice with her sword, severs the head, tumbles the body off, and takes the canopy, later shown with the head.

l: Israelite attack on the Assyrian camp, Judith
s: has_planned_outcome Assyrians flee and are pursued [Judith's plan] Judith lays out the plan: at morning the men take up arms and go out with a captain as though going down to the plain, but do not descend. The Assyrians would rouse their captains, find Holofernes missing, and flee, and Israel would pursue them. In this unit the Israelites go out in bands to the mountain ascents, and the Assyrians see them and take them to be coming down to battle, while the attack itself has not yet been carried out.

The plunder is the thirty-day looting of Asshur's camp by Bethulia's people, enriching them greatly as hill-country and plain villages and cities also take spoils; Holofernes' tent and furnishings go to Judith.

All the women of Israel run together to see Judith, bless her, and make a dance for her. Judith gives branches to the women, and she and those with her make garlands of olive. She leads all the women in the dance, and all the men of Israel follow in armor with garlands and songs in their mouths.

l: pursuit and slaughter of the enemy, Judith
s: extends_to Damascus [pursuit continued beyond Damascus and its borders] After the enemy flees, the Israelite warriors rush upon them, and Ozias sends word to Betomasthaim, Bebai, Chobai, Chola, and every border of Israel to destroy the enemy. The Israelites strike them to Chobai, and people from Jerusalem, the hill country, Gilead, and Galilee fall on their flank with great slaughter until they are past Damascus and its borders.

Asshur leads an Assyrian army from the northern mountains, vast enough to stop torrents. He threatens to burn Israel's borders, kill young men, and seize infants and virgins, but the Almighty Lord brings him to nothing by a woman's hand.

is_a song of praise sung by all the people in Israel Judith begins the song in all Israel, and all the people sing it with loud voices. It calls for timbrels and cymbals, recounts the defeat of Asshur by a woman, praises the Lord as great creator and merciful to those who fear him, and ends by warning that nations against Israel will suffer fire and worms in judgment.

This document is the Book of Psalms, chapters 1 to 150, a collection of Hebrew prayers, laments, hymns and wisdom poems addressed to the LORD. Many carry headings naming David, the sons of Korah, Asaph, Solomon, Moses, Heman and Ethan, and instructions for the Chief Musician. The Songs of Ascents (120 to 134) form a distinct group. The central figures are the LORD, who is refuge, shepherd, judge and King, and David, who speaks most often, frequently pursued by enemies such as Saul, Absalom and Doeg. Israel, Zion and Jerusalem, and the contrast between the righteous and the wicked, recur throughout. It opens with Psalm 1, which contrasts the blessed man, a tree by streams, with the wicked, who are like chaff. Psalm 2 then presents the LORD's Anointed King set on Zion. The first long stretch (3 to 41) is mostly David's prayer. He laments enemies, confesses sin (32, 51), asks for vindication, and affirms trust. Notable pieces include the creation and law hymn (19), the suffering and praise of 22, the shepherd psalm (23), and the entry of the King of glory (24). Psalms 42 to 89 add Korah and Asaph material. These include longing for God, national laments over defeat and the destroyed sanctuary, a wedding song for the king (45), the refuge psalm (46), Zion celebrations, a prayer for a just king (72), and Asaph's struggle over the wicked's prosperity (73). Psalms 78 and 105 to 106 retell Israel's history, with God's wonders and the people's repeated rebellion, while 88 ends in unrelieved lament and 89 turns from praising David's covenant to complaint. Psalm 90, attributed to Moses, reflects on human brevity. Psalms 91 to 100 stress the LORD's reign, security under him, and calls for all the earth to worship. Psalms 101 to 119 include David's vows, praise of God's mercy and creation (103, 104), the priest-king oracle (110), the long acrostic on God's law (119), and thanksgiving. The Songs of Ascents express trust, joy and longing for Zion, and Psalm 137 mourns exile in Babylon. Psalms 138 to 145 return to David's prayers for deliverance and praise. The book closes with five hymns (146 to 150) summoning all creation, with instruments and every breath, to praise the LORD.

The blessed man does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, stand on the path of sinners, or sit in the seat of scoffers. His delight is in the LORD's law, on which he meditates day and night. He is likened to a tree planted by streams of water that yields fruit in season and whose leaf does not wither, and whatever he does prospers.
The wicked, unlike the blessed man, are likened to wind-driven chaff; they will not stand in judgment or among the righteous, and their way will ultimately perish.
is_known_by LORD [LORD knows their way] The righteous have a congregation in which sinners will not be able to stand. The LORD knows their way.

LORD is the central deity of these records, which read as a sequence of psalms. He is not human, though the opening units first suggested a person. He is portrayed as a sovereign, eternal God: enthroned in heaven and Zion, King forever, Most High, and creator of the heavens, earth, sea, moon and stars. He owns all of it, and he rules and judges the nations in righteousness and equity. He is righteous, holy, good, faithful, merciful, gracious and slow to anger, and his loving kindness endures forever. He loves justice and righteousness. He hates the wicked and workers of iniquity, and he will destroy them. The records begin with the LORD knowing the way of the righteous, laughing at rebellious kings, and decreeing that his Anointed is his son and King on Zion, with the nations as inheritance. Much of the early and middle material is David's personal relationship with him. David calls him shield, glory, rock, fortress, stronghold, high tower, deliverer, redeemer and refuge. The LORD hears and answers David's cries, sustains him, forgives his sin, and will not leave his soul in Sheol. He shows David the path of life, though David also protests that he hides his face and afflicts him. He is also a shepherd who guides, restores and provides for the speaker. He defends the poor, needy, fatherless, oppressed and brokenhearted, and he shelters those who fear him and take refuge in him. The middle sections widen to the national story. He chose Zion and Jacob, made a covenant with David, and later seems to reject his anointed. He brought Israel out of Egypt with plagues, divided the Red Sea, led them through the wilderness, gave them the land, and forgave and judged them. Later psalms proclaim that he reigns and will judge the earth, and they celebrate his creation and providence. They also celebrate his rescue of wanderers, prisoners and seafarers, his forgiveness and redemption of Israel, and his building up of Jerusalem. The records close with a call for all creation to praise him in his sanctuary for his mighty acts and excellent greatness.

The LORD's law is what the blessed man delights in and meditates on day and night. It is described as truth and everlasting righteousness, settled in heaven forever, and worth more than thousands of pieces of gold and silver. It teaches the disciplined man and lights the psalmist's path toward a blameless life, blessing, peace, and understanding.

The Anointed is the target of the kings' and rulers' plotting alongside the LORD. He is identified as the King the LORD has set on Zion, and as the son to whom the LORD gives the nations as an inheritance and the earth's far reaches as a possession. He is to break the nations with a rod of iron and dash them like a potter's vessel, and the kings are told to give homage to the Son, lest his wrath be kindled; those who take refuge in him are blessed.

is_in_state raging [plotting a vain thing] The nations are described as raging, and the peoples as plotting a vain thing. The LORD promises them to his son as an inheritance, and they are to be broken with a rod of iron and dashed in pieces like a potter's vessel.

The kings of the earth, with rulers, take a stand and conspire against the LORD and his Anointed, seeking to break their bonds. They are then commanded to be wise, serve the LORD with fear, and honor the Son lest they perish.

Zion is the holy hill and city of God, a place whose foundation is in the holy mountains and about which glorious things are spoken. It is chosen by the LORD, loved above all the dwellings of Jacob, and declared his resting place forever. Praise waits for God there, and vows are performed. The records trace its fortunes: it is established by the Most High, and a set time comes for the LORD to show mercy to it, with his servants cherishing its stones and dust. The LORD builds it up and appears in glory, and peoples and kingdoms gather to serve him. Those who return are brought back to it in dreamlike wonder. Yet it is also hated by enemies, and exiles by the rivers of Babylon remember it and the songs once sung of it. Finally the LORD promises to bless its provision, satisfy its poor with bread, and clothe its priests with salvation, so that its saints shout aloud for joy.

A vain plot by nations, peoples, kings and rulers to break the bonds and cast off the cords of the LORD and his Anointed. The LORD answers with laughter, derision, anger and wrath, installing his King on Zion; persisters perish, while those taking refuge in the Son are blessed.

David is a person presented throughout these records as the attributed author of many psalms and prayers, the son of Jesse, father of Absalom, servant and anointed king of the LORD, and shepherd of Israel. The records open with him fleeing his son Absalom, yet unafraid of tens of thousands against him, trusting the LORD as shield and sustainer. What matters most is the recurring pattern of his life: he is hunted, afflicted and surrounded by enemies, pursuers, betrayers and false witnesses, and he responds by taking refuge in the LORD, pleading for mercy and deliverance, and ending in confidence and vows of thanks. His distress is vivid: he is faint, with troubled bones, nightly tears, sorrow, mourning, and a desolate heart. He is poor and needy, imprisoned in a cave, and forgotten by those around him. He also confesses sin, including his great iniquity, his sin against God after Nathan came to him over Bathsheba, and his being born in iniquity. At the same time he claims integrity, avoids the wicked, loves the LORD's house, delights in the saints, and shows compassion by fasting for enemies when they were sick. The records tie particular songs to episodes: Cush the Benjamite, pretending insanity before Abimelech, Doeg's report to Saul, the Ziphites telling Saul where he hid, being seized by the Philistines in Gath, fleeing Saul in the cave, Saul's men watching his house, and the desert of Judah. Deliverance from Saul and all his enemies leads to his being made head of the nations, served by foreigners, and appointed firstborn, highest of the kings of the earth, who will call the LORD Father and rock of his salvation. Later records stress God's choice of him from the sheepfolds, the LORD's oath that his descendants will sit on his throne, and his own oath to find a place for the LORD. The final records return to prayer for rescue, with his hatred of the wicked, his awareness that he is fearfully and wonderfully made, his thirst for God, and his identity as the LORD's servant, rescued from the deadly sword and vowing a new song.

David's adversaries have increased and many rise up against him, and many say of him that there is no help for him in God. They are said to have set themselves against him on every side in tens of thousands. David says the LORD has struck all his enemies on the cheek bone and broken the teeth of the wicked.

The sons of men are accused by David of turning his glory into dishonor, loving vanity, and seeking falsehood. He then urges them to stand in awe, not sin, reflect quietly, offer righteous sacrifices, and trust the LORD.

Sacrifices of righteousness are offerings God will delight in. David says God does not want mere sacrifice; the true sacrifices are a broken, contrite spirit. The psalm closes promising delight in righteous offerings, burnt offerings, and bulls on his altar.
The psalmist, beset by enemies, prays to the LORD in the morning and bows in reverence at God's holy temple.
The psalmist's enemies are unfaithful in speech, flatter with their tongues, harbor destruction in their hearts, and stand in rebellion against the LORD.
cannot_dwell_with LORD cannot_stand_before LORD [the arrogant]

l: righteous (those who take refuge in God), Psalms
s: takes_refuge_in LORD loves LORD [loves his name]

Sheol is the place of the dead, where no thanks are given to the LORD. In Chapter 49 the foolish are appointed there like a flock, their beauty decaying far from their mansions, though God redeems the psalmist's soul; in Chapter 88 Heman's life draws near it.
David's adversaries, called workers of iniquity, cause his grief that wastes his eye; he commands them to depart and wishes them ashamed, dismayed, turned back, and suddenly disgraced.

l: suffering and anguish (David's illness and grief), Psalms
s: David's suffering is described as faintness, troubled bones, great anguish of soul, weariness from groaning, and nightly weeping that floods his bed and drenches his couch. His eye wastes away and grows old with grief because of his adversaries. He asks the LORD for healing and relief, and ends by affirming that the LORD has heard his weeping.

David's prayer in this psalm consists of pleas that the LORD not rebuke him in anger, that he have mercy, heal, return, deliver, and save him, and that his enemies be shamed. He argues that the dead cannot remember or thank the LORD. The psalm closes with David declaring that the LORD has heard his supplication and accepts his prayer.

David's pursuers are those he asks to be saved from, who he fears will tear apart his soul like a lion with no one to deliver. He calls them adversaries raging against him and asks the LORD to lift himself up against their rage.

l: unrepentant man (wicked person who is judged), Psalms
s: An unrepentant man is warned that God prepares sword, bow and flaming arrows against him. He conceives mischief, travails with iniquity, brings forth falsehood, and digs a pit; ultimately he falls into it, and his trouble and violence return on his own head.

Man is the psalmist's subject of wonder: why the LORD cares for him. Made a little lower than the angels and crowned with glory and honor, he is then given rule over the LORD's works, with animals, birds, and sea creatures put under his feet.

The heavens are described as the work of the LORD's fingers, containing the moon and the stars which he ordained. The LORD's glory is set above them. The psalmist considers them as the occasion for wondering about man's place.

The nations are portrayed as forgetters of God, mere humans. The LORD rebukes them and erases their name forever; they fall into their own traps, David asks they be judged and humbled, and they are turned back to Sheol.
The wicked, in Chapter 9, are destroyed by the LORD and snared by their own handiwork, finally turned back to Sheol together with all nations that forget God.

David's enemies turn back, stumble, and perish in the LORD's presence. They are overtaken by endless ruin, and even the memory of the cities overthrown is said to have perished. David also describes those who hate him as causing his affliction.

has_refuge_in LORD [high tower] The oppressed are promised that the LORD will be a high tower for them in times of trouble. The afflicted are not forgotten, and the needy and poor will not always be forgotten nor their hope perish forever.

David, author of a psalm, is afflicted by those who hate him. He thanks the LORD wholeheartedly, rejoices and sings praise, then pleads for mercy and rescue from death's gates, vowing to declare praise and rejoice in salvation in Zion.

Judgment is carried out and prepared by the LORD, who sits on his throne judging righteously and will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in uprightness. He has already executed judgment and made himself known, and David asks that the nations be judged in his sight.

The wicked are an arrogant group who prey on the helpless, sneering at adversaries and condemning the LORD while leaving no room for God in their thoughts. Prosperous and certain they will never be shaken or held to account, they ambush and murder the innocent like a lion. Yet they are caught in their own nets, and the speaker asks the LORD to break their arm until no wickedness remains.

l: the helpless (victims of the wicked), Psalms
s: The helpless are hunted, ambushed, caught in the wicked man's net, crushed, and made to collapse and fall under his strength. The speaker asks the LORD not to forget them, and affirms that the LORD helps the victim and the fatherless and hears the desire of the humble, with the hope that the fatherless and oppressed will be judged and terrified no more.

The wicked are a group who bend bows to shoot secretly in darkness at the upright in heart. The LORD hates them, and their destined portion is blazing coals, fire, sulfur, and scorching wind rained upon them.

l: the righteous (the upright in heart), Psalms
s: will_see LORD [sees his face] The upright in heart are the targets of the wicked, who aim to shoot at them in darkness. The question is raised of what the righteous can do if the foundations are destroyed, yet the LORD examines them and the upright are promised that they will see his face.

l: godly and faithful (the godly man), Psalms
s: state ceasing [fail from among the children of men] The godly man is said to cease and the faithful to fail from among the children of men, which is the speaker's reason for crying out for help. Their disappearance is presented as the opening crisis of the psalm.

The wicked flatterers and boasters speak with flattering lips and a double heart, claiming their tongues will prevail and no one is lord over them. The speaker asks the LORD to cut off their lips and tongues. The psalm closes noting the wicked walk everywhere while vileness is exalted.
The weak are oppressed and the needy groan. Because of this, the LORD declares he will arise and set the oppressed one in safety from those who malign him.
The LORD's words are flawless, likened to silver refined seven times in a clay furnace, and are affirmed to be kept and preserved from this generation forever.

is_practiced_by children of men [everyone lies to his neighbor] Everyone is said to lie to his neighbor, speaking with flattering lips and a double heart. The speaker asks the LORD to cut off all flattering lips and the boasting tongue, and the LORD's pure words stand in contrast to this deceit.
David's enemy is said to be triumphing over him. David prays that the enemy and his adversaries will not say 'I have prevailed against him' or rejoice when David falls.

God, called the LORD, LORD of Armies, Most High, Mighty One and God of Jacob, Abraham and Israel, is the central figure of these psalm records. He is a living God, the light, salvation, strength, rock, fortress and refuge of David and of the speakers, a very present help in trouble, and a helper who sustains, redeems and delivers. He hears prayer, knows the secrets of the heart and the psalmist's sins, desires truth in the inward parts, and does not despise a broken and contrite heart. He needs no sacrifices, since the world and all creatures are his. He is also a great King and judge over all the earth, enthroned forever on his holy throne, dwelling in Zion and Salem, feared by kings, and exalted above the nations. He judges peoples with equity, rewards each according to his work, ends wars by breaking bow and spear, and destroys the wicked and enemies of his people. The records unfold in a rough arc. They begin with the fool who denies him and with David's trust in him as light and salvation. Speakers then thirst for him, ask why he has forgotten or rejected them, and recall how he drove out nations and planted his people. Next come celebrations of his kingship, his refuge in Zion, and his claims over the nations. Cries for deliverance and personal confession follow, with assurance of his loving kindness, truth and help. Later psalms praise his creation, rule over seas and mountains, provision of rain and harvest, care for the fatherless and widows, and his acts at the sea, in the wilderness and in the choice of Judah, Zion and David. Laments recur that he has rejected, scattered or been angry with his people, and the speakers plead for restoration. The records close with God presiding over the assembly and judging the gods, being asked not to keep silent against enemies, and being trusted to tread down adversaries so that all know he alone is the Most High over all the earth.

The fool is a figure who says in his heart there is no God. Across both chapters, he is described as corrupt, guilty of abominable deeds, with no one doing good; the portrayal repeats consistently from beginning to end.

The workers of iniquity are rebuked as ignorant: they devour God's people like bread and never call on the LORD. They are said to be in great fear, since God is with the righteous, while they frustrate the poor's plan.
Children of men, examined by the LORD looking down to find any who understand and seek God, are found all gone aside, together corrupt, with no one doing good.

God's people are the LORD's heritage, his own people and the sheep of his pasture, who made them. Much of the record shows them suffering: workers of iniquity devour them like bread, and the wicked break them in pieces, afflict them, and murder the widow, alien and fatherless. They are held in captivity, yet God defends them, will not reject or forsake them, and is expected to restore their fortunes and bring them back. The account ends with judgment returning to righteousness, willing offering in holy array, and thanksgiving and praise at his gates.

Israel is the people of God, identified throughout these records with Jacob, the house of Jacob, and the houses of Aaron and Levi, and spoken of both as a collective and as a single person ("his troubles"). It is God's inheritance, possession, dominion, servant, and a people near to him, whose praises God inhabits. It dwells in Judah and has David as its shepherd. The records open with a hope: Israel will be glad and rejoice when the LORD restores his people's fortunes, and salvation is wished to come out of Zion. The story begins in Egypt. Israel came into Egypt, grew greater than its adversaries, and was hated. God then brought it out with a strong hand, through the Red Sea and the wilderness, and gave it the lands of Sihon, Og, and Canaan under an everlasting covenant, so that it might keep his statutes. Its fathers trusted and were delivered. Israel is repeatedly urged to trust, hope in, and praise the LORD, who is its help and shield. Festival worship is a statute and ordinance for it, and God has shown his word to Israel as to no other nation. The record is not only favorable. Israel repeatedly tested and rebelled against God, with high places and engraved images. It was disobedient and did not listen, so God gave it over to its own stubborn counsels and to the sword. God also testifies against his people in judgment, saying he does not need their offerings, and calls them to thanksgiving and vows. Israel is afflicted from its youth, with its back plowed, yet has not been prevailed against. Enemies rise up, conspire to destroy it as a nation, and covet its pasture lands, but the LORD's help is in his name. The records move toward redemption: God gathers Israel's outcasts, is asked to redeem it from all its troubles, and will redeem it from all its sins. Israel is urged to hope in the LORD from now and forevermore. It ends in praise: God lifts up Israel's horn, and Israel and the children of Zion rejoice in their King with dance, tambourine, and harp.

Jacob is a patriarchal figure whose descendants, Israel, are the LORD's chosen, a generation seeking Him; the covenant was confirmed to him as a statute, and he lived in Ham's land when Israel entered Egypt.

The salvation of Israel is a hoped-for deliverance, wished for in the closing verses of Chapters 14 and 53, that would come out of Zion. It is tied to the LORD restoring and bringing back his captive people, resulting in rejoicing and gladness.

The sanctuary, also called the LORD's holy hill, is the place the psalmist asks about when he asks who may dwell or live there. The unit gives the qualifications for those who may stay in it, and the one who meets them will never be shaken.

l: righteous person (who may dwell with the LORD), Psalms
s: This person walks blamelessly, does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart. He does not slander, harm his friend, or cast slurs against his fellow man, despises a vile man, honors those who fear the LORD, and keeps an oath even when it hurts. He does not lend money for usury or take a bribe against the innocent, and he will never be shaken.

is good [lines fallen in pleasant places] The LORD assigned David's portion and cup and made his lot secure. David says the lines have fallen to him in pleasant places and that he has a good inheritance.

The wicked oppress David and surround him and those with him, closing up their callous hearts and speaking proudly with their mouths. They set their eyes to cast David and his company down to the earth. They are compared to a greedy lion or a young lion lurking in secret places, and are called men of the world whose portion is in this life.

The prayer is introduced as A Prayer by David and is offered as a righteous plea from lips without deceit. It asks for a hearing, vindication, protection, and deliverance from enemies, and it ends with confidence that David will see the LORD's face and be satisfied.

David's enemies, described as strong, hateful, and too mighty for him, came on him in his day of calamity. With the LORD's help David pursued, struck, and crushed them like dust before the wind. They cried out but received no answer from the LORD, and foreigners came trembling out of their strongholds and submitted to David.

l: theophany (the LORD's descent in storm), Psalms
s: In response to David's cry, the LORD bowed the heavens and came down amid a shaking earth, smoke, consuming fire, thick darkness, and thick clouds. He rode on a cherub on the wings of the wind, thundered with hailstones and coals of fire, and sent out arrows and lightning bolts. At his rebuke the channels of waters appeared and the foundations of the world were laid bare.

The LORD's deliverance of David: sent from on high, he drew David out of many waters from enemies too mighty for him, brought him to a large place out of delight, supported him in calamity, and gives lasting deliverance to David and his offspring.

David's righteousness is his claim of blamelessness: he kept the LORD's ways, ordinances and statutes, avoided iniquity, and had clean hands. In Chapter 18 he says the LORD rewarded him accordingly, reflecting that the LORD is merciful, perfect and pure to the pure, shrewd to the crooked.

The heavens, also called the expanse, declare God's glory and show his handiwork. Day after day and night after night they pour out speech and knowledge, their voice reaching all the earth, and God has set a tent in them for the sun.

The sun is a heavenly body given a tent by God, likened to a bridegroom leaving his room and a strong man rejoicing in his course, travelling from one end of the heavens to the other; its heat reaches everything.

The LORD's law is perfect and restores the soul, belonging to him alongside his covenant, precepts, commandment, fear, and ordinances, all sure and true. It is more desirable than gold, sweeter than honey, warns the psalmist, and keeping it brings great reward.

David, the psalmist and servant of the LORD, whose rock and redeemer is the LORD. Warned by the LORD's law and rewarded for keeping it, he asks forgiveness for hidden errors, restraint from presumptuous sins, and acceptable words.

The king is the LORD's anointed, for whom worshippers pray: that he be answered in trouble, set on high, and granted his heart's desire. His offerings are to be remembered; they affirm the LORD saves him, and close by calling on him.

A group of worshippers who pray blessings on the king, vow to triumph in his salvation, and raise banners in God's name. They trust the LORD's name over chariots and horses, stand upright, and finally cry out for the LORD to save and the King to answer.

l: those who trust in chariots and horses (the enemies), Psalms
s: Enemies who trust in chariots and horses instead of the LORD; in the end they are bowed down and fallen, unlike the worshippers who stand upright.

The king is a ruler who rejoices in the LORD's strength and salvation and trusts in him. The LORD grants his request for life forever, sets a fine gold crown on him, and gives glory, honor and majesty. Through the Most High's loving kindness he is unmoved, made most blessed forever and glad in God's presence.

The LORD's enemies hate him and intended and plotted evil against him that cannot succeed. His hand will find them out, and he will make them like a fiery furnace in his anger, with fire devouring them. Their descendants will be destroyed from the earth, and they will be made to turn their backs when he aims drawn bows at their faces.

The psalmist, named in the heading as David, is a despised sufferer who calls himself a worm, scorned by people and surrounded by mocking enemies. He has trusted the LORD since birth, pleads for deliverance, and ends by vowing to praise God's name in the great assembly.

The psalmist's enemies see him, mock him, insult him with their lips, and shake their heads, taunting that if he trusts the LORD, the LORD should rescue him. They are pictured as many bulls of Bashan, roaring lions, dogs, and a company of evildoers who pierce his hands and feet, stare at him, and cast lots for his clothing.

l: those who fear the LORD (worshippers), Psalms
s: is_called_to praise LORD [fear him] Those who fear the LORD are called to praise, glorify, and stand in awe of him, and the psalmist promises to pay his vows before them in the great assembly. The humble among them are promised that they will eat and be satisfied and praise the LORD, and that their hearts will live forever.
